articles.title: From ad to offer

body.support:
Getting a job takes five steps.

**1. Decode the ad.** Find a real ad. Circle what they **must** have. Notice their words, like *reliable*.

**2. Tailor your resume.** For each thing they want, add a real example from your life.

**3. Write a cover email.** Short and **formal**:

- **Subject:** *Application: Kitchen Hand – Kai Thompson*
- *Dear Ms Rossi,*
- Which job you want.
- Two reasons you'd be good, with examples.
- When you can work.
- *Kind regards,* and your name.

Attach your resume.

**4. Interview.** Use your STAR stories. Ask a question.

**5. Follow up.** Say thank you. No reply in a week? Send one polite email.
body.core:
Getting a job isn't one big moment. It's five small steps, and each one uses something you've already learnt.

**1. Decode the ad.** Find a real ad you'd actually apply for. Circle the **essential criteria** (what they *must* have), the desirable ones, the hours, and how and when to apply. Notice the exact **words** they use: *reliable*, *fast-paced*, *customer service*.

**2. Tailor your resume.** Don't send the same resume everywhere. For each thing the ad needs, find real **evidence** from your life, and put it where they'll see it. If the ad says *customer service*, your canteen shift belongs near the top. Use their words, but only if they're true. Your **transferable skills** count: teamwork from sport, responsibility from caring for siblings.

**3. Write a cover email.** Keep it short and **formal**:

- A clear **subject line**: *Application: Casual Kitchen Hand – Kai Thompson*
- A formal greeting: *Dear Ms Rossi,* (or *Dear Hiring Manager,*)
- Which job, and where you saw it.
- Two reasons you suit the job, each with evidence matched to the ad.
- Your availability.
- A polite close: *My resume is attached. I'd welcome the chance to talk with you.*
- *Kind regards,* and your name.

Check spelling, attach your resume as a PDF with your name in the file name, and send it from a sensible email address.

**4. Nail the interview.** Prepare your three STAR stories, re-read the ad, and plan a question to ask. Speak clearly, and say it back if you're unsure.

**5. Follow up.** Send a thank-you the same day. If you've heard nothing after a week, send one polite check-in. Then keep applying: every application is practice.

A note on AI tools: they can help you check spelling, but employers can spot a generic email. Your words, your real examples, every time.
body.extend:
Getting a job takes a sequence of linked texts, all written for the same reader: the employer.

**1. Decode the ad.** Find the **essential** and desirable **criteria**, the conditions and the application process. Note the employer's key words: they show what the employer values.

**2. Tailor the resume.** Match each criterion to specific **evidence**, and put the most relevant first. Use the employer's terms where they're accurate. Show **transferable skills** from school, sport, volunteering or family.

**3. Compose a cover email.** A brief, **formal** text with a clear structure:

- an informative **subject line**
- a formal salutation
- an opening identifying the role and where it was advertised
- two claims, each substantiated with evidence matched to the criteria
- availability
- a courteous close and sign-off.

Formal language does more than sound polite. It shows you as a professional before you've even met. Proofread, attach a clearly named PDF, and use a sensible email address.

**4. Prepare the interview:** STAR stories mapped to the criteria, delivery, and a question of your own.

**5. Follow up:** a same-day thank-you, then one courteous check-in after about a week. Track your applications.

AI tools can help with proofreading. But generic text with no evidence weakens an application. Your real evidence is what makes you stand out.

caseStudies.title: Who gets the entry-level jobs?

body.support:
A government group studies jobs. In **2025**, it asked bosses about jobs for people **starting out**.

What it found:

- These jobs are most common in **shops**, **labouring** and **care** work.
- City bosses had fewer of them.
- About **1 in 3** bosses gave these jobs to people who **had worked before**.

So show what you can do. Use examples from sport, school and home.
body.core:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** is a government agency that studies jobs. It asks employers about hiring. In **December 2025**, it shared what they said about **entry-level** jobs: jobs for people just starting out.

Here's what it found:

- Entry-level jobs were most common in **sales**, **labouring**, and **care and service** work, like hospitality.
- Employers in **capital cities** had the most jobs. But they were the **least likely** to offer entry-level ones.
- Employers in the **country** were more open to people starting out.
- About **1 in 3** employers gave an entry-level job to someone **with experience**.

So a job that says *no experience needed* can still go to someone who has some. That's why you tailor. You may not have work experience. But you have **evidence**: sport, school, helping out, caring for family. Show it clearly, in their words.
body.extend:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** (JSA) surveys Australian employers about hiring. A **December 2025** report looked at **entry-level** jobs in cities and in the regions.

- Entry-level jobs were most common for **sales workers**, **labourers** and some **care and service** roles. Professional jobs were much harder to get into.
- Employers in **capital cities** had the most jobs. Yet they were the **least likely** to offer entry-level ones. Country employers were more open to beginners. One reason: less competition.
- About **1 in 3** employers hiring for entry-level roles took on **experienced** candidates.

So *entry-level* doesn't mean *no competition*. Without work history, you compete with skills from the rest of your life. Present them as evidence, matched to what each employer asks for.

**Subject:** Application for Casual Sales Assistant

Dear Ms Rossi,

I would like to apply for the Casual Sales Assistant job at Rossi's Hardware, which I saw on SEEK.

Your ad asks for someone reliable who enjoys helping people. I have volunteered at my local Men's Shed for a year, helping visitors find tools and parts. I have never missed a Saturday.

I am free after 3:30 pm on weekdays and all day on weekends.

My resume is attached. I would love the chance to meet you.

Yours sincerely,
Eli Brown
0400 000 000

teacher.overview: A Crossroads capstone combining Work Ready and Your Voice. Students complete a full application for a real (or realistic) local job: decoding the ad, matching their evidence to its criteria, tailoring their resume, writing a formal cover email, doing a structured mock interview and following up. The literacy focus is adapting a sequence of linked texts for one reader: evidence selection, formal register, and spoken delivery. The case study is Jobs and Skills Australia's December 2025 data on entry-level jobs.
prep: Collect real, current local job ads suitable for 15–17 year olds (retail, hospitality, supermarkets, sport, care).
Line up interviewers: other staff, a panel, or local employers. Even one visitor makes it real.
Make sure every student has a draft resume (from Build Your Resume) and three STAR stories (from Nail the Interview).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The plan
steps: **Hook (10 min):** two cover emails, one generic and one tailored. Which gets the call?
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Decode and match
steps: **Step 2: match me to the ad (20 min).** Conference: is every piece of evidence real and specific?
**Case study (15 min):** who gets the entry-level jobs?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Tailor and write
steps: **Tailor the resume (15 min).** Move the most relevant evidence to the top.
**Anatomy of a cover email; Send it or fix it? (15 min).**

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — The interview
steps: **Prepare (10 min):** STAR stories mapped to the ad; one question.
**Do it: mock interviews (40 min).** Rotate through a panel.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Follow up
steps: **Level Up, reflect (15 min):** quick check; request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** decode, tailor, email, interview, follow up. Cover email: subject line, formal greeting, which job and where, two matched reasons with evidence, availability, polite close and sign-off. Each employer needs different things; generic applications don't show you meet their criteria.

**Cover email:** 1 subject line; 2 formal greeting; 3 which job and where; 4 evidence matched to the ad; 5 availability; 6 polite close and sign-off.

**Sort:** “hey, saw ur ad” — fix; clear opening — send; “I reckon” — fix; specific availability — send; “Cheers mate” — fix; resume attached — send.

**Case study:** entry-level jobs most common in sales, labouring, community and personal service; capital city employers least likely to offer entry-level roles; about 1 in 3 hired experienced candidates. Employers may prefer lower training costs or less risk. Evidence: sport, school roles, volunteering, caring, projects.

realityCheck: **Real applications are real.** Only send applications to real employers if the student genuinely wants the job and you've agreed. Otherwise, “send” it to you.
**Some students can't work yet** (age, family or study). They still complete the full run for a realistic future job.
**Rejection happens.** Frame every application as practice; praise the process, not just offers.
**Unpaid trials.** Remind students that a trial must be short, supervised and only to show skills (see Crack the Job Ad).
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the payoff for Work Ready and Your Voice, and some students will get real jobs from it.
